meta.tagline: Brick streets where independence was born, mural walls and a cheesesteak wit

pills: The city where America was born
The mural capital of the world

overview.title: Welcome to Philadelphia
overview.intro: Philadelphia is America's birth room: the Declaration was signed here, the Liberty Bell cracked here, the Constitution was written here. But Philly doesn't pose with its history — it keeps its working-class soul in four thousand painted murals, the stall hum of Reading Terminal, the rowhomes of the southern neighborhoods and an accent that says 'jawn'. Someone still runs the Rocky steps every morning, and 'wit or witout' is still a serious exam at the steak counters. Philly doesn't try to impress you; it just is itself — and that's exactly why it's loved.

local_word.definition: The miracle of Philadelphia English: a word that can replace anything. An object, a place, an event, a person — all are jawn. 'Pass me that jawn', 'that jawn was crazy'. Linguists study it, Philadelphians wield it with pride — there is no other word like it in the world.

rules.title: Arrange the independence tickets ahead
rules.description: Independence Hall runs on timed free tickets: in season they're gone by early morning, so reserve online. The Liberty Bell needs no ticket but its queue stretches by noon — set both for the first hours, and let history be told without the crowds.

rules.title: Prepare for the cheesesteak exam
rules.description: The order is short and sharp: 'one whiz wit' (Cheez Whiz, onions) or 'provolone witout'. The counter moves fast and indecision holds the line — skip the tourist duel for the neighborhood masters; Philly's true steak lives there.

rules.title: Read the walls: murals are the key to the city
rules.description: Forty years of the Mural Arts program turned the city into the world's largest open-air gallery: over four thousand walls. Build your route on the murals — every neighborhood's wall tells its own story, and you read the city's history from the sidewalk.

quick_facts.label: Signature
quick_facts.sub: The signing room of the Declaration

tip.label: The Philly philosophy
tip.text: This city takes pride in being unpolished: it tells its history for free, paints its art on walls and wraps its food in paper. Trade expectations of polish for authenticity — once Philly trusts you, it tells you America's best story.

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.intro: Philly is compact and walkable: the historic district is on foot, SEPTA's subway and buses link the rest, and Indego bikes fill the gaps.

items.title: Arriving from the airport
items.description: From PHL the SEPTA Airport Line reaches Center City in 25 minutes: cheap and painless. Ride apps run 20–40 minutes by traffic — the train wins at most hours.

items.title: The walkable core
items.description: From Old City to Rittenhouse, City Hall to the southern neighborhoods, Center City is toured on foot: the grid plan makes getting lost difficult. The historic district is fully pedestrian — comfortable shoes befriend the brick.

items.title: SEPTA subway and buses
items.description: Two subway lines (orange north-south, blue east-west) do a visitor's work: practical for the stadiums and the museum district. Key card or contactless — for Fishtown, the blue line plus a walk is the formula.

items.title: Indego bikes
items.description: Share stations spread through the center: the Schuylkill river trail offers flat, scenic pedaling from the museum to Boathouse Row. The riverbank is Philly's calmest transit line.

items.title: Between the rivers
items.description: On the Delaware side, Race Street Pier and the summer hammocks of Spruce Street Harbor Park; on the Schuylkill side, the museum axis: moving between two rivers is the natural rhythm of a Philly day.

callout.label: River trail tip
callout.text: In the late afternoon drop onto the Schuylkill Banks boardwalk: joggers, rowing shells and Boathouse Row lighting up at dusk. Start behind the art museum and walk to the South Street bridge — Philly's most graceful hour passes on this bank.

stay.title: Where to Stay
stay.intro: In Philly the choice is a choice of texture: Old City's historic brick, Rittenhouse's elegant square, Fishtown's young energy.

local_word.definition: Philadelphia's shoulder-to-shoulder row houses: seventy percent of the city lives in them. Marble stoops, twin-windowed facades and neighborhood loyalty — the rowhome is not just housing but the unit of Philly social life. Sitting on the stoop watching the street is a legitimate evening plan.

items.name: Old City
items.description: Walking distance to Independence Hall and Elfreth's Alley: galleries, brick lanes and First Friday art nights. The natural base for a history-first visit.

items.name: Rittenhouse Square
items.description: Polished hotels, restaurants and boutiques around the square's plane trees: Philly's most refined corner. Everything within a walk — comfort and location at their peak.

items.name: Midtown Village
items.description: 13th Street's restaurant row, City Hall next door and both subway lines in reach: a practical, lively base. Dinner at the doorstep.

items.name: Fishtown
items.description: The old workers' quarter transformed: music venues, third-wave coffee and award-winning kitchens. Ten minutes to the center on the blue line — Philly's creative present.

items.name: University City
items.description: The world of Penn and Drexel across the river: museums, a botanical garden and student-priced tables. Five minutes to the center by train — the calm, economical side.

best_time.title: When to Go
best_time.intro: Philly lives four full seasons: spring blossoming and fresh, summer humid and festive, autumn golden, winter harsh but museum-friendly.

items.label: Spring
items.name: Cherry Blossoms and Squares
items.subtitle: Spring · Blossoming parks, fresh walking air
items.description: April's cherry blossoms dress Fairmount Park, the squares refill, and the historic district hits its most comfortable touring weather. The crowds stay below summer levels — spring Philly fully delivers on the walking-city promise.

callout.label: April tip
callout.text: In early April visit the cherry grove around Shofuso, the Japanese house: Fairmount's little-known corner becomes a pink festival. Pair it with a Boathouse Row walk home — spring Philly's most graceful half day.

items.label: Summer
items.name: Humid and Festive
items.subtitle: Summer · Hot days, riverside evenings, July 4th
items.description: Summer Philly is humid but generous: the hammocks of Spruce Street Harbor Park, open-air cinemas, and the main stage of July 4th — in the city where independence was born, the celebration carries a different charge.

callout.label: July 4th tip
callout.text: Live Independence Day where it began: daytime events in the historic district, an evening concert and fireworks before the art museum. Spot-claiming starts at noon — Philly is this holiday's host, and takes it seriously.

items.label: Autumn
items.name: Golden Brick Season
items.subtitle: Autumn · Crimson parks, crystal air, football Sundays
items.description: October is Philly's peak: the Wissahickon valley turns crimson, brick facades glow in golden light, and coffee season opens. On Eagles game days the city wears green — the 'Go Birds' greeting opens every door.

callout.label: October tip
callout.text: In mid-October walk Wissahickon Valley: a canyon, a creek and crimson forest inside the city — the Forbidden Drive trail is car-free and serene. Coffee afterwards on Chestnut Hill's stone-housed main street.

items.label: Winter
items.name: Museums and the Ice Rink
items.subtitle: Winter · Cold days, warm museums, a riverside rink
items.description: Philly winter is cold but its program is rich: the vast art museum, the Barnes collection and Reading Terminal's warm stalls. An ice rink rises on the Delaware — and when snow falls, the brick streets turn to postcards.

callout.label: January tip
callout.text: On a cold morning run the Rocky steps: no tourists in winter, and the victory pose is all yours. The reward is inside — the museum's collection wants a full day; check the Sunday 'pay what you wish' hours.

eat.title: What to Eat
eat.intro: The Philly table is set with working-class classics: meat in pressed bread, pretzels in paper, a hundred kitchens in one market — plain and filling.

local_word.definition: The constitution of the cheesesteak order: 'wit' means with onions, 'witout' without (Philly's pronunciation of 'with'). At the counter you name the cheese first, then the onion verdict: 'whiz wit' is the classic of classics. A fast, clear order is Philly respect — decide while you're still in line.

items.name: The cheesesteak
items.description: Thin-sliced beef, melting cheese and an Italian roll: the city's signature. Whiz, provolone or American — the debate is endless, the flavor guaranteed. The neighborhood steak shops stay a step ahead of the tourist duel.

items.name: The roast pork sandwich
items.description: The locals' quiet favorite: slow-roasted pork, sautéed broccoli rabe and sharp provolone. The masterpiece in the cheesesteak's shadow — the master at Reading Terminal earns his lunch queue.

items.name: A Reading Terminal crawl
items.description: The market open since 1893: Amish stalls, a hundred kitchens and historic neon. Breakfast to dessert under one roof — the midday crowd is part of the atmosphere; claim your table first.

items.name: The soft pretzel morning
items.description: The Philly pretzel is thin, soft and figure-eight shaped: hot from the morning bakery, with mustard. The city averages a pretzel a day per person — fill your quota.

items.name: The hoagie
items.description: Cold cuts, cheese, lettuce and oil-vinegar in an Italian roll: Philly's sandwich heritage. The old-school Italian hoagie comes from a deli counter — the official food of picnics and riverbanks.

items.name: Water ice and Tastykake
items.description: 'Wooder ice' from the corner shop in summer, Tastykake from the market year-round: Philly's sweet identity. Mango or cherry — the spoon is small, the nostalgia enormous.

callout.label: Table rule
callout.text: Philly food is unpolished and should stay that way: a paper-wrapped sandwich, a plastic table and a fast counter are the finest packaging for flavor. Eat from the stalls at the Italian Market and Reading Terminal; save the smart dinner for Fishtown's award-winning kitchens.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Corners
hidden_gems.intro: Everyone sees the Liberty Bell; these six are Philly's mosaic-clad, creek-voiced hidden face.

items.name: Magic Gardens
items.description: The mosaic labyrinth artist Isaiah Zagar wove on South Street over thirty years: mirror shards, bottles and folk art in a two-story dream courtyard. Philly's most photogenic half hour — book the ticket ahead.

items.name: Elfreth's Alley
items.description: Continuously inhabited since 1703: thirty-two Georgian houses, cobblestones and flowered windows. Go early — America's oldest 'neighborhood' will be yours alone.

items.name: The 9th Street Italian Market
items.description: One of America's oldest open-air markets: cheesemongers, butchers, taquerías and barrel fires. Italian heritage and Mexican present at the same stall — Saturday morning is its liveliest hour.

items.name: Wissahickon Valley
items.description: An 800-hectare forest valley at the city's edge: a creek, stone bridges and the car-free path of Forbidden Drive. The Philadelphian's nature refuge — it turns to crimson festival in fall.

items.rarity: A string of lights on the river
items.name: Boathouse Row at night
items.description: The Victorian rowing clubs on the Schuylkill are outlined in thousands of bulbs at night: the reflection on the water is the city's most romantic frame. Watch from the west bank or the Spring Garden bridge.

items.name: The Fishtown and Kensington murals
items.description: Mural Arts' boldest walls stand in the northern neighborhoods: giant portraits, neighborhood stories and factory facades. On a guided mural tour or your own route — the city's gallery is free.

callout.label: Street strategy
callout.text: Philly's pearls come at street scale: Elfreth's in the morning, the Italian Market at noon, Magic Gardens in the afternoon, Boathouse Row at night. No car needed — this city opens to the walker, brick by brick.

traps.title: Tourist Traps
traps.intro: Philly is an honest city; its traps feed on the tourist's hurry — know these four.

items.name: Getting stuck in the Pat's vs Geno's duel
items.description: Hours pass in the queues of the two neon tourist counters; the cheesesteak is above average, the experience is a photo shoot.
items.instead: Take the photo, eat the sandwich at a neighborhood master: the counters of South Philly and Reading Terminal are both queue-free and superior. A 'whiz wit' order earns the same respect everywhere.

items.name: Arriving unplanned at Independence Hall
items.description: The timed free tickets vanish by morning in season: the walk-up visitor is left photographing the building from outside.
items.instead: Reserve online days ahead (for a token fee) or take the first-hour window at the desk. The Liberty Bell needs no ticket — queue for it before noon, after the Hall tour.

items.name: Melting time in the Rocky queue
items.description: The selfie line at the statue reaches half an hour at midday; the steps run gets squeezed by the crowd.
items.instead: Come at 08:00: the steps are empty, the victory pose is yours, the statue line is three people. And take the reward — the museum itself is among America's best; see more than the steps.

items.name: Insisting on a car in Center City
items.description: Narrow streets, one-ways and expensive garages: downtown, a car is not freedom but an hourly expense.
items.instead: Walk the center and link the far neighborhoods with SEPTA and Indego. A car makes sense only for Wissahickon or a suburban trip — rent for that day, walk the rest.

callout.label: Golden rule
callout.text: In Philly, history and art are largely free: the Hall ticket costs nothing, the murals live on the street, and the Bell queue yields to patience. Save the money for market stalls and a Fishtown dinner — this city budgets for authenticity, not show.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Itineraries
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. Times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: From independence to the mosaic garden

steps.title: The Rocky steps and museum morning
steps.description: Run the steps and strike the victory pose on an empty plaza; at this hour there's no statue queue.

steps.title: Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell
steps.description: See the signing room with your timed ticket, then face the bell's crack: America's birth certificates on one square.

steps.title: Elfreth's Alley and Old City
steps.description: Walk America's oldest street and browse the gallery windows: brick Philly's most graceful corner.

steps.title: Reading Terminal lunch
steps.description: A crawl of the market stalls: the roast pork sandwich or an Amish breakfast. Claiming a table is a sport; the atmosphere is the prize.

steps.title: Magic Gardens and South Street
steps.description: Get lost in the mosaic labyrinth, then continue through South Street's shops: Philly's most colorful face.

steps.title: Cheesesteak and river night
steps.description: Take the 'whiz wit' exam at a neighborhood counter; close with the Boathouse Row lights reflected on the river.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: History, walls and valleys — the full Philly

steps.title: Classic Philly
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: the Rocky morning, Independence Hall, Elfreth's, Reading Terminal, Magic Gardens, a cheesesteak night.

steps.title: Art and neighborhoods
steps.description: The art museum's collection in the morning (or the Barnes' impressionists); a Rittenhouse Square lunch; the Italian Market and South Philly murals in the afternoon; an award-winning Fishtown kitchen + music venue at night.

steps.title: Valley and farewell
steps.description: A morning walk on Wissahickon's Forbidden Drive; Chestnut Hill's stone main street and coffee at noon; the chilling corridors of Eastern State Penitentiary in the afternoon; a farewell hoagie picnic at the Schuylkill sunset.

phrases.title: 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: The Philly accent is confident and direct; these five phrases warm the city to you at jawn speed.

items.meaning: The miracle word that replaces anything — every sentence can be built with 'that jawn'
With / without onions — the constitution of the cheesesteak order
The Philly pronunciation of 'water' — 'wooder ice' is the summer classic
The plural 'you' — 'youse guys' is the signature of Philly street speech
The Eagles greeting — on game day one sentence makes you the city's friend
